_provenance.discipline: The Stage 3 fact-check is the load-bearing input here. It flagged the Stage 1 central thesis ('the bill splits the office, not the appointment route' / 'zero changes to who picks the prosecutor') as OVERCLAIM and MISLEADING_FRAMING. The proposed Public Prosecutor route is NOT identical to the Attorney-General's Article 145(1) PM-advice route: AG Dusuki publicly said (Bernama, 23 Feb 2026) the bill makes no provision for the PM in PP appointment, and the proposed route runs YDPA-in-discretion on JLSC recommendation after consulting the Conference of Rulers. Synthesis rebuilds the editorial spine on verified ground: separation is real reform; the contested question is whether routing the PP through the JLSC (which the AG sits on) WITHOUT a parliamentary confirmation vote is enough to insulate the office, the exact check the Bar Council (14 Mar 2026 motion) and the ten Rafizi-led PKR MPs (24 Feb 2026) demanded and were not seated on the committee to argue. Royalty discipline retained: the Yang di-Pertuan Agong and Conference of Rulers appear only as constitutional functionaries under Articles 138/139/145, never characterised. The revised PSSC bill text is NOT public; cards never assert what the revised bill contains, only what was tabled and what was demanded.

headline: The AG-prosecutor split returns after eight years. Who confirms the new prosecutor stays unsettled.
context: On 18 May 2026 the parliamentary committee chaired by Azalina Othman Said held its sixth meeting on the bill to separate the Attorney-General and Public Prosecutor, fused in one office since 1957. She called it 'the best compromise'. The report is not public.

cards.big: Malaysia will split the Attorney-General and Public Prosecutor for the first time since 1957. Splitting the office is the easy part; deciding who confirms the new prosecutor is not.
cards.sub: The 2018 Pakatan Harapan manifesto promised to separate them 'immediately'. Eight years and four AGs later, Azalina calls it 'the best compromise'. The bill returns 22 June.

cards.big: Article 145 has placed prosecution and the government's legal advice in one executive-appointed officer since 1957. The bill finally separates the two.
cards.sub: Article 145(1) puts the Attorney-General's appointment with the Yang di-Pertuan Agong on the Prime Minister's advice. Article 145(3) gives that one officer discretion to start or drop criminal cases.

cards.big: Ten government MPs led by Rafizi Ramli demanded a Dewan Rakyat vote to confirm the new prosecutor. None were named to the committee that shaped the compromise.
cards.sub: On 24 February 2026 the ten PKR backbenchers asked for a public confirmation hearing and a parliamentary vote before any nominee reaches the Agong. The committee seated other MPs.

cards.big: The new prosecutor would be recommended by the Judicial and Legal Service Commission, the body the Attorney-General sits on. As tabled, the bill added no parliamentary vote.
cards.sub: Attorney-General Dusuki says the bill gives the Prime Minister no role in choosing the prosecutor. The Bar Council's reply: the AG's seat on that commission keeps executive influence in the room.

cards.big: Separation is not independence. The office split has consensus; the vote to let Parliament confirm the prosecutor does not, and its backers were kept off the committee.
Picture giving the umpire his own office, then still choosing him through a panel the team captain sits on, with no open vote on the pick.
cards.sub: The bill creates a standalone prosecutor. The commission that recommends the prosecutor still includes the Attorney-General.

cards.big: Splitting the office is the reform everyone could agree on. The harder one, a confirmation vote to insulate the prosecutor, went to a committee the MPs who asked for it were left off.

introduced_claims.claim: The Attorney-General and Public Prosecutor have been combined in one office since 1957.
introduced_claims.primary_source: Federal Constitution of Malaysia, Article 145; Constitution in force 31 August 1957. Stage 3 verified Article 145(1)/(3) text (m_true 0.9).

introduced_claims.claim: Attorney-General Dusuki said the bill gives the Prime Minister no role in choosing the Public Prosecutor.
introduced_claims.primary_source: Bernama, 23 February 2026, reported in Stage 3 omitted_facts: 'AG Tan Sri Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar said the bill makes no provision for the Prime Minister in the appointment of the Public Prosecutor.'

introduced_claims.claim: The new Public Prosecutor would be recommended by the Judicial and Legal Service Commission, on which the Attorney-General sits.
introduced_claims.primary_source: Federal Constitution Article 138(2) (AG/Solicitor-General membership of the JLSC), verified by Stage 3 (m_true 0.86); proposed PP route via JLSC recommendation per Malaysian Bar resolution cited in Stage 3.

synthesis_notes: Over-integration decision: Stage 1 ran a sharp 'unchanged appointment route / zero changes' thesis; Stage 3 rated that central thesis MISLEADING/OVERCLAIM. I did not average. I sided fully with Stage 3 and rebuilt the spine, because the formal PP appointment route demonstrably differs from the AG's 145(1) route (Dusuki/Bernama) and the honest, still-sharp angle is independence-not-separation, anchored on (a) the JLSC route with the AG seated on it, (b) the absence of a parliamentary confirmation vote in the bill as tabled, and (c) the exclusion of the dissenting MPs from the committee. All three are verified and require no claim about the unreleased revised bill text. Compression decision: the Legal fact sub says 'criminal cases' rather than enumerating the Article 145(3) Syariah/native/court-martial carve-outs; the carve-outs are not load-bearing to the point (breadth of ordinary-prosecution discretion) and 'criminal cases' avoids overstatement. Completeness gap preserved: no card asserts the revised PSSC bill omits parliamentary confirmation (text not public); cards are time-anchored to 'as tabled' (27 Feb 2026) and to the demand made on 24 Feb 2026. The 'best compromise' is reported as Azalina's phrasing, not as fact. sr scored 85: strong, balanced integration that corrected a central overclaim and added the government's defence, capped below 90 by the residual completeness gap (revised bill text unavailable) that no synthesis can close without the document.
